questions.question: A student types `ok <- true` (lower case), intending to store a logical value in `ok`. What does R do?
options: It stores the logical value `TRUE`, since R ignores case in logical values.
It stores the text `"true"`, since an unquoted word is read as a string.
It looks for an object named `true`, finds none and stops with an error.
It stores `NA`, since `true` is not one of the valid logical values.

questions.question: Running `"2" + 1` stops with `Error in "2" + 1 : non-numeric argument to binary operator`. Why does R refuse this addition?
options: The quotation marks make `"2"` a character string, and `+` does not accept text.
`+` joins text only with other text, so the `1` would also need quotation marks.
Double quotation marks make text, but single quotes as in `'2' + 1` would give a number.
R first turns `"2"` into `NA`, and adding `1` to `NA` is not allowed.

questions.question: In R, `TRUE + TRUE` returns `2`. What does `is.numeric(TRUE)` return, and why?
options: `TRUE`: logical values are stored as the integers 1 and 0, so they count as numeric.
`TRUE`: the addition changed the stored constant `TRUE` into the number 1.
`FALSE`: `TRUE + TRUE` gives an integer, and integers do not count as numeric.
`FALSE`: `TRUE` is stored as a logical value and becomes 1 only inside the arithmetic.

questions.question: An object is created with `x <- 7L`, and later the line `x <- 7.5` is run. Which statement about `x` afterwards is correct?
options: It is a double holding 7.5; the new assignment replaces both value and type.
It is an integer holding 7, since `x` keeps the type it was created with.
It is an integer holding 7.5, since only the value is replaced, not the type.
The second line stops with an error, as an integer object cannot take a decimal.

questions.question: To check that a count computed as `n <- 3 * 4` is a whole number, a student runs `is.integer(n)`. What does the call return, and what does that show?
options: `TRUE`: 12 has no fractional part, so it is a whole number.
`FALSE`: it tests the storage type, and `3 * 4` without `L` is a double.
`TRUE`: `is.numeric(n)` is `TRUE`, and every numeric value is an integer.
`TRUE`: R prints `n` as `12`, not `12.0`, which marks an integer.
